# Heartwood ESP32

> Nostr private keys stored on computers are one browser exploit away from theft. Heartwood ESP32 is a hardware signing device that keeps your nsec permanently on a microcontroller: private keys never leave the chip, and signing outside an installed policy requires physical button approval.

Status: beta. Keep an independent recovery copy and use small values while the complete destructive cross-board recovery matrix remains unfinished.

Heartwood targets Nostr developers and self-hosters who want hardware-grade key custody. It uses the nsec-tree hierarchical derivation scheme to manage multiple Nostr identities from a single master secret, with per-identity child keys derivable on demand. Supported boards: Heltec WiFi LoRa 32 V3/V4 (ESP32-S3, OLED), LilyGO/TENSTAR T-Display (classic ESP32, colour TFT, two buttons), Waveshare ESP32-C6-LCD-1.47 (RISC-V), plus a USB-tethered ESP8266 signer from a separate in-repo crate.

Two deployment modes ship from the same firmware, selected at runtime from the NVS network config:

- **USB-bridged (high-assurance default)**: USB-attached to a Pi running `heartwoodd`, all radios disabled, holds the master secrets. The Pi is zero-trust: all serial traffic is NIP-44 ciphertext, so a compromised Pi cannot extract keys or widen policy; already-authorised clients still receive signatures their installed policy permits.
- **WiFi-standalone (opt-in)**: the ESP32 joins WiFi and talks to Nostr relays directly, running the full NIP-46 signing loop on-chip with no Pi. Stores up to eight WiFi networks; tries visible saved networks strongest-first (saved order breaks ties) and roams on a sustained 10 dB advantage (two consecutive scans); reordering never resends passwords (per-SSID `keep` semantics). Relay-side management (kind 24134) is authenticated to a provisioned operator pubkey and replay-protected.

## Getting Started

Requires the ESP Rust toolchain (`espup install`). Build per board with the wrapper script, which pins the matching cargo feature, target triple, and sdkconfig fragment:

```bash
./scripts/build-firmware.sh v4 --release        # Heltec V4 (default); also v3, tdisplay, c6
espflash flash firmware/target/heartwood-v4.elf
./scripts/build-firmware.sh tdisplay --release  # T-Display (classic ESP32, 4 MB layout)
espflash flash firmware/target/heartwood-tdisplay.elf
./scripts/build-firmware.sh demo --release      # board-check demo game (not the signer)
```

The wrapper writes the board-tagged ELF to `firmware/target/heartwood-<board>.elf` (`<board>` is the argument you passed). Flash that, not a path under `firmware/target/<triple>/`: the target triple differs per board (`xtensa-esp32s3-espidf` for Heltec, `xtensa-esp32-espidf` for T-Display, `riscv32imac-esp-espidf` for C6). The Heltec boards use `firmware/partitions.csv` (two 2 MB A/B slots); the 4 MB boards use `firmware/partitions-4mb.csv` (one 3 MB slot), and for their first flash the Sapwood web flasher or the release's esp-idf-generated bootloader and partition-table binaries are safer than passing the CSV to `espflash` (see `.github/workflows/release.yml`). The crates are independent, so build the host tools from their own directories; `README.md` has the full build, run and quick-start steps.

Easiest end-user path: the Sapwood web console (https://sapwood.forgesworn.dev) flashes, provisions, and updates devices over Web Serial from CI-built, ed25519-signed releases.

## Key Concepts

- **nsec-tree derivation**: HMAC-SHA256 keyed derivation producing deterministic child keys from a master secret via a `purpose/label` path (e.g. `persona/social`). Compromise of a child never threatens the root.
- **Policy engine**: Per-master, per-client approval: exact v2 policies bound method + event-kind sets for unattended signing; everything else needs the display + button. Physical approval is a 2-second hold; on two-button boards the second button is an explicit cancel and the screen labels both.
- **Multi-master NVS**: Up to 8 master identities. Provisioning modes: `bunker` (raw nsec), `tree-mnemonic` (BIP-39), `tree-nsec`.
- **Per-client persona consent**: each pairing holds up to eight client credentials and sixteen explicit client/persona grants; consent can be withdrawn for one persona on one device, all personas on one device, or every device in the pairing.
- **Encrypted at rest (opt-in)**: Seeds sealed under a PIN or a host-held 32-byte vault key; a locked WiFi device announces a per-boot unlock pubkey (kind 24135) and receives the key from the operator (kind 24136). FIRMWARE_INFO and get_status report the mode directly (`at_rest`: `none`/`pin`/`vault`/`encrypted`, plus `unlock_phone_count`, `null` over damage), so a manager never has to guess it — see `docs/SECURITY-MODEL.md` for the digest-bound marker and self-repair behind `pin`/`vault`. **Downgrade warning:** on a board with a PIN or vault key, turn it off before flashing beta.16 or older (`0.18.0-beta.16` and earlier). From beta.17, seeds are sealed as 82-byte `HWDK` blobs under a random data key (`common/src/data_key.rs`), and the first unlock on beta.17 or later migrates older records in place; earlier firmware only reads the 92- and 101-byte per-seed records (`common/src/seed_cipher.rs`), so it cannot read the sealed seeds. To turn it off, unlock the board, then send `SET_PIN` (0x25) with an empty payload ("Remove PIN?") or `VAULT_SET` (0x62) with an empty payload ("Disable vault?"; `heartwoodd --vault-disable` does this for a vault); each needs a button hold, stores every seed in plaintext and drops the enrolled phone records, so re-enrol phones if you turn it back on. A WiFi-mode board refuses the change while it holds bearer notes ("at-rest changes need USB mode while notes are held"), so empty the note locker or switch to USB mode first.
- **Phone unlock**: up to 16 enrolled phones can unlock a locked WiFi board. Per phone, the board posts a kind-24135 from its per-boot one-time key with only an `["h", hint]` tag and sealed content (`t` = `locked`); the phone answers with a kind-24136 from a throwaway key. When the relay list changes, the board posts the same message with `t` = `relays` on the relays the phones were last told about, so they follow it; a phone never prompts for that. A phone is added over USB (frame 0x64) or, on firmware advertising `phone_enrol_relay_v1`, over the relay with the `enrol_unlock_phone` management method (Cambium 0.6.0 or later; 0.7.0 can also scan a code from Sapwood; bench-run with Sapwood and Cambium 0.7.1 in `docs/HARDWARE-TEST-CHECKLIST.md` section 29): device operator only, one-time mutation challenge, and still a press on the board, whose card leads with five spoken-token words derived from the phone's one-off enrolment key; the owner holds only if the phone shows the same five words, which are the only defence against a swapped key (the check code shown after the press confirms delivery, not origin). This firmware must ship together with the Cambium and Sapwood changes that show those words and keep labels to printable ASCII. Wire format and vectors: `common/src/phone_unlock.rs`, `common/tests/fixtures/phone-unlock-v1*.json`; when and where updates go: `common/src/phone_relays.rs`. FIRMWARE_INFO and get_status also report `phone_relays` (`current`/`pending`/`unknown`), the same idiom as `at_rest` above, so a manager can show "phones not yet told" while a relay change is still stranding an enrolled phone on relays the board has since left; `pending` clears once an old relay has accepted an update for that change (later rounds still run regardless), not once every update round has run, and can persist indefinitely if every old relay is dead or refuses the delivery: the only way out then is revoking and re-enrolling the phones.
- **NVS scrub**: ESP-IDF leaves a deleted or replaced NVS value's bytes on flash until the sector is collected, so the firmware zeroes every entry NVS has marked erased: at boot, after a phone or pairing revoke, an identity removal and every at-rest change. `get_status.capabilities` carries `nvs_scrub_v1`; `revoke_unlock_phone` (and `revoke_client`, to the device operator) answer with `scrub: {zeroed, pages_skipped, complete}`, and FIRMWARE_INFO reports the last pass as `nvs_scrub`. What it does and does not remove: `docs/SECURITY-MODEL.md` (*Leftover bytes in NVS*); logic and power-cut tests: `common/src/nvs_scrub.rs`.
- **Frame protocol**: Binary serial protocol shared by every host tool: magic `0x48 0x57`, 1-byte type, 2-byte big-endian length (at most 32768), payload, 4-byte big-endian CRC-32 (IEEE, as in zlib) over type, length and payload. Type codes are in `common/src/types.rs`; `README.md` lists the common ones.
- **Signed OTA**: Releases are ed25519-signed in CI; the device verifies signature + SHA-256 and rolls back automatically. Heltec boards carry 2 MB A/B slots; 4 MB boards (T-Display, C6) update via a host-side app-only reflash instead.

## API Surface

| Crate | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| `common` | Shared crypto: nsec-tree derivation, NIP-44/NIP-04, NIP-46 types, frame protocol, policy + net-config types |
| `firmware` | ESP32 firmware for all boards, plus the `heartwood-demo` board-check game bin |
| `heartwoodd` | Pi/host daemon: Hard mode (bridges a USB device) and Soft mode (software-backed signer, no ESP32) |
| `provision` | Host CLI: provision, generate, restore, and manage client slots over USB serial |
| `sign-test` | End-to-end harness: sends NIP-46 requests over serial |
| `ota` | Host-side serial OTA tool with SHA-256 verification |
| `ota-sign` | Release-key tool: keygen / sign / verify for firmware images |
| `esp8266-firmware` | Bare-metal USB-tethered signer for the ESP8266 |

The `common` crate has two signing backends: `k256-backend` (pure Rust, host tools/tests) and `secp256k1-backend` (libsecp256k1 C FFI, alignment-safe on Xtensa, required for firmware). Both produce identical outputs, pinned by a frozen test vector.
